questions.question: You are working on a project with a tight deadline, and a team member is falling behind on their tasks. What do you do?
options: Ignore it and focus only on your own tasks to ensure you finish on time.
Complain to the manager about the team member's slow progress.
Reach out to the team member privately, ask if they are facing blockers, and offer to help if possible.
Take over their work without telling them so the project doesn't fail.
questions.explanation: Offering help privately fosters teamwork and directly addresses the blocker without unnecessary escalation.

questions.question: A client requests a major feature change just days before the scheduled release. How do you handle it?
options: Tell the client it's impossible and refuse to make the change.
Acknowledge the request, assess the impact on the timeline and budget, and present the trade-offs to the client and manager.
Work overtime in secret to try and squeeze the feature in without telling anyone.
Implement the change but delay the release indefinitely until it's done.
questions.explanation: Professionalism requires assessing impact and communicating trade-offs rather than flatly refusing or working in secret.

questions.question: You discover a critical bug in the code you just deployed to production, but nobody else has noticed it yet. What is your next step?
options: Quietly fix it over the weekend so nobody finds out.
Immediately notify your team and manager, explain the impact, and propose a rollback or hotfix plan.
Wait to see if any users actually complain about it before taking action.
Blame the QA team for not catching it during testing.
questions.explanation: Transparency and swift communication are key to resolving production issues effectively.

questions.question: You have two high-priority tasks assigned to you by two different managers, and both are due by the end of the day. You cannot complete both. What do you do?
options: Pick the one you like doing the most and ignore the other.
Work on both at the same time, delivering rushed and low-quality work for both.
Bring the two managers together (or email them both) to explain the conflict and ask them to prioritize which task takes precedence.
Clock out at 5 PM regardless of what is finished.
questions.explanation: Communicating priority conflicts to management ensures expectations are aligned and business needs are met.

questions.question: During a team meeting, a colleague presents an idea that you strongly disagree with. How do you respond?
options: Interrupt them immediately to explain why their idea won't work.
Say nothing during the meeting, but complain about it to other coworkers later.
Wait for them to finish, acknowledge the merits of their idea, and respectfully present your alternative perspective with evidence.
Agree with them just to avoid conflict, even though you know it's a bad idea.
questions.explanation: Constructive, respectful feedback after listening creates a healthy collaborative environment.

questions.question: You are assigned a task using a tool or technology you have never used before. How do you proceed?
options: Refuse the task because you weren't trained for it.
Accept the task, spend some time reading the documentation, and ask a knowledgeable colleague for a brief overview if you get stuck.
Guess how it works and hope for the best.
Spend weeks trying to master the tool before starting the actual task.
questions.explanation: Taking initiative to learn while knowing when to ask for help demonstrates resourcefulness.

questions.question: You receive negative feedback from your manager regarding a recent presentation you gave. What is your reaction?
options: Get defensive and explain why they are wrong.
Feel demotivated and stop putting effort into future presentations.
Listen carefully, ask clarifying questions to understand how you can improve, and apply the feedback next time.
Blame the audience for not understanding your presentation.
questions.explanation: Receiving feedback constructively shows a growth mindset and professionalism.

questions.question: Your team is adopting a new workflow process that you think is less efficient than the old one. What should you do?
options: Continue using the old process secretly.
Give the new process a fair try, gather objective data on its inefficiencies, and present your findings constructively to the team.
Complain loudly in team chats about how terrible the new process is.
Quit the team.
questions.explanation: Providing data-driven, constructive feedback is much more productive than silent rebellion or loud complaining.

questions.question: A coworker frequently interrupts you while you are doing deep, focused work. How do you handle it?
options: Yell at them to leave you alone.
Politely explain that you are in the middle of focused work and ask if you can catch up with them at a specific time later.
Put on headphones and completely ignore them when they speak to you.
Stop what you are doing every time and let your own work suffer.
questions.explanation: Setting polite but firm boundaries ensures both communication and productivity are maintained.

questions.question: You notice that a process your team uses daily is highly repetitive and prone to human error. What is your approach?
options: Accept that this is just how things are done here.
Research a way to automate or streamline the process, create a small proof-of-concept, and present it to your manager.
Refuse to do the process until someone else fixes it.
Complain to HR about the working conditions.
questions.explanation: Proactively solving inefficiencies demonstrates value and technical leadership.
